extracted.intended_audience: aspiring creative writers, especially those interested in nature writing and creative nonfiction
extracted.subtask_description: Personal-essay reflections on craft and habits for creative nonfiction/nature writers, drawing lessons from Annie Dillard's The Writing Life and other works. Emphasizes writerly habits, voice development, attention to environment, and emotional honesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live in the world; be careful what you read and learn
rubrics_metrics.description: “The writer studies literature, not the world. He lives in the world; he cannot miss it. If he has ever bought a hamburger, or taken a commercial airplane flight, he spares his readers a report of his experience. He is careful of what he reads, for that is what he will write. He is careful of what he learns, because that is what he will know.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not substitute secondhand literary study for direct experience. Pay attention to lived detail without turning work into mere reportage; curate what you read and learn because those choices shape what you can write.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write about what perplexes, amazes, and bewilders you (not just 'what you know')
rubrics_metrics.description: Dillard told the author not to write about what she knows but to 'write about the things that perplexed me, amazed me, bewildered me' and to 'chase them... until they made sense to me.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subjects that provoke genuine curiosity or puzzlement; pursue them deeply and persistently rather than recycling familiar, comfortable material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write as if you were dying — prioritize urgency and significance
rubrics_metrics.description: “Write as if you were dying. At the same time, assume you write for an audience consisting solely of terminal patients... What would you begin writing if you knew you would die soon? What could you say to a dying person that would not enrage by its triviality?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for work that feels necessary and avoids trivialities; cultivate an urgency that forces clarity about what truly matters in your subject and voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcend immediate experience — write about places/times you haven't lived
rubrics_metrics.description: “Write about winter in the summer. Describe Norway as Ibsen did, from a desk in Italy; describe Dublin as James Joyce did, from a desk in Paris... Walt Whitman rarely left his room.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not limit yourself to literal firsthand experience; imaginative displacement (time, place) is legitimate and can yield convincing, resonant writing when handled attentively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the material shape you — fit yourself to the 'paint'
rubrics_metrics.description: “The painter, in other words, does not fit the paints to the world. He most certainly does not fit the world to himself. He fits himself to the paint.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow subject matter to dictate tone, form, and approach rather than forcing a preconceived style onto it; adapt your voice to the needs of the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize process over declared intention
rubrics_metrics.description: Dillard's notes indicate that process, not intention, produced works (e.g., about The Living: 'I talked myself into writing an old-fashioned novel. But it was the process that got her there, not her intention.').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trust iterative practice and discovery in drafting; allow surprises and emergent structure rather than rigidly executing an initial plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embrace vulnerability — use 'embarrassing' nonfiction honestly
rubrics_metrics.description: Dillard conceives The Writing Life as 'embarrassing nonfiction narrative' and the author notes that this vulnerability is what makes the work speak warmly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honest self-revelation can create warmth and identification. Risk exposing weakness or uncertainty when it serves the truth of the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use imitation consciously to find your voice
rubrics_metrics.description: “Unconscious imitation is a powerful tool. Once you know that you are using it, you can use it... You begin to write in the voices that you’re reading. You do this enough and eventually you break into your own style, your own voice, your own method.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitate admired writers as a learning technique, but remain aware of when imitation becomes unconscious mimicry; move from imitation to original voice intentionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend closely to environment and unexpected events
rubrics_metrics.description: Dillard’s practice included writing about whatever happened in her environment over a few days — an exercise that led to unpredictable material (e.g., 'and then a plane crashed nearby').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe quotidian details and be open to chance occurrences; letting such events into your work can generate powerful, authentic moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissolve boundaries — write from a multi-self or interconnected perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: The author describes Dillard’s boundary-challenging as 'boundary-dissolving' — 'The reason why I feel like she is inside me when I read her work is because she and I aren’t separate people. That boundary of selfhood is imaginary: I am you, you are me, and we are also the trees.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment with perspectives that blur self/other and human/nature distinctions to deepen resonance and empathy in nature writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert intellectual passion into physical, disciplined craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Dillard writes about the necessity of 'days of solitary confinement' and 'The task was to change intellectual passion to physical energy and some sort of narrative mastery, from a standing start.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop routines of concentrated, solitary practice to translate ideas into polished narrative; discipline transforms enthusiasm into craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read broadly but follow curiosity rather than rigid sequence
rubrics_metrics.description: The author contrasts a friend's disciplined, sequential reading of an author's catalogue with her own haphazard, heart-led approach: 'I am digging at random. I am reading wherever my heart takes me next.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow your reading to be guided by interest and emotional resonance; serendipitous reading can prime new directions in your writing.
